title: In Defence of the Placebo

lines.text: Good afternoon. Today I'd like to defend a word that doctors usually use as an insult. The word is 'placebo', and I'd like to persuade you that it deserves rather better treatment.

A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient: a sugar pill, a saline injection, an inert cream. In trials, it's the thing we compare real drugs against. For most of history it has been the villain, the noise you have to subtract.
But look at what the villain does. In many trials, patients given a placebo improve, sometimes markedly, especially where the symptom is subjective: pain, nausea, fatigue, low mood.
Please note my wording. The placebo doesn't shrink a tumour or mend a bone. What it seems to alter is the experience of symptoms, which is, from the patient's point of view, not a trivial matter.

Part of the effect is not mysterious at all. Many illnesses fluctuate. If you take a pill when you feel worst, you'll probably feel better soon, and the pill gets the credit. Statisticians call that regression to the mean, and it's responsible for a great many miraculous cures.
But that isn't the whole story. Even when you control for it, there's an effect that appears to depend on expectation, on ritual, on the attentive voice of someone in a white coat.

The most intriguing finding, to my mind, comes from small trials in which patients were told, openly, that they were receiving a placebo. Some of them, with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, still reported improvement.
I'd urge caution. The trials were small and the results need replication. I'm not proposing that we hand out sugar pills and send everyone home.

There's an obvious ethical worry. If a doctor gives a patient a placebo without saying so, that's deception, and deception corrodes trust. The honest version, by contrast, would seem to preserve the benefit and the relationship.
Whether it does is an empirical question, and I'd be delighted to be proved wrong either way.

Now, a thought about what this means for ordinary medicine. If expectation and attention have an effect, then a doctor who listens, explains and reassures is, in a quite literal sense, part of the treatment.
I find that both obvious and neglected. Everyone agrees that bedside manner matters. Few health systems pay for it.
This puts me in an awkward position. I'm asking you to take seriously a thing I can't prescribe, can't patent and can't bottle.
Which is, I'm told, a poor business model, and a rather good argument for kindness.
For next week, read the two papers on open-label placebo trials, and decide whether you'd be willing to enrol, as a patient, in one.
Thank you. I'd be grateful if you would not now all report feeling much better, merely because I've told you I'm a professor.

questions.q: How does the lecturer regard the trials in which patients knew they were taking a placebo?
options: Convinced that sugar pills cure illness
Indifferent to whether it works
Dismissive of the whole approach
Intrigued, yet careful about the small samples
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Las encuentra interesantes pero con cautela: 'The most intriguing finding' y 'I'd urge caution. The trials were small'.

questions.q: What does she imply by saying 'Few health systems pay for it'?
options: Doctors refuse to be paid for listening
Health systems undervalue what they say matters
Bedside manner is not important to patients
Few health systems exist in the world
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Todos dicen valorar el trato médico, pero casi nadie lo financia: 'Everyone agrees that bedside manner matters. Few health systems pay for it.'

questions.q: She says that a placebo seems to change mainly how symptoms are experienced.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'What it seems to alter is the experience of symptoms'.

questions.q: Why does she mention regression to the mean?
options: To criticise the language of statisticians
To show that illnesses stay constant
To prove that placebos never work
To explain why some improvement is not caused by the pill
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Explica que parte de la mejoría es natural: 'you'll probably feel better soon, and the pill gets the credit'.

questions.q: How should her closing remark about not reporting feeling better be understood?
options: As a genuine request for honest feedback
As a humorous nod to the effect of authority
As a complaint about students' health
As a warning about the exam
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Bromea con que su autoridad de profesora podría actuar como placebo.

questions.q: She says that a placebo can shrink tumours.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'The placebo doesn't shrink a tumour or mend a bone.'

dictation: The placebo doesn't shrink a tumour or mend a bone.
Few health systems pay for it.

title: Hamlet in a Supermarket

lines.text: My guest this evening is a theatre director who has set Hamlet in a corporate headquarters, Macbeth in a petrol station and, if I have it right, A Midsummer Night's Dream in a branch of a supermarket. Julian Frost, have you no shame?
None whatsoever, though I'd say in my defence that the supermarket was rather well lit.
Is it ever a gimmick?
Often, and I've been guilty. A modern setting is a gimmick when it's a costume the play doesn't fit. It's a good idea only when it reveals something that the original setting hid.
Give me an example of that.

In Hamlet, the court is a place of surveillance. Everyone is listening at doors and reporting to everyone else. We reached for a world of cameras, security passes and sleek glass walls, and suddenly the plot looked less like a legend and more like Tuesday.
Less like a legend and more like Tuesday. You'd put that on a poster.
My producer would rather put a star on a poster.
Do audiences complain that the language doesn't match the setting? Somebody speaking in verse while holding a clipboard?

Occasionally. But I think it's a surprisingly small problem. The verse has a strange effect: in a modern room, it makes the characters sound like people whose feelings are too large for their circumstances. Which, frankly, is exactly right.
And the purists?
They write to me. Some of the letters are very beautiful. One gentleman told me that I'd 'taken a cathedral and filled it with fridges'.
How did you reply?
I said that cathedrals were once full of noise, merchants and dogs, and that the quiet we revere is a rather recent invention. He did not write again.
Do you think that was a victory?
Not at all. I think he's probably still composing a response, and I'd rather like to read it.
Is there a play you'd never modernise?
I'd never say never, but I'd be careful with anything where the setting is the argument. If a play is about a particular law, or a particular crisis, moving it can empty it of its point.
And a play you'd love to?
Any of them, if I could find the right reason. The test is simple. Ask what the new setting lets the audience see, and if the answer is 'it's different', save your money.
Julian Frost, thank you.
Thank you. And do tell the supermarket I'm still waiting for my discount.

questions.q: What is Julian's attitude to the charge that modern settings can be gimmicks?
options: He is proud of every modern setting he has chosen
He admits he has sometimes been guilty of it
He blames audiences for demanding them
He denies that gimmicks ever occur
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Es autocrítico: 'Often, and I've been guilty.'

questions.q: What does Julian imply by saying that the plot looked 'more like Tuesday'?
options: The story felt familiar rather than distant
The legend was found to be boring
The production was set on a particular day
The play had been shortened
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La trama pasó de leyenda lejana a algo cotidiano y reconocible: 'less like a legend and more like Tuesday'.

questions.q: Julian says that a modern setting works when it reveals something the original hid.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'It's a good idea only when it reveals something that the original setting hid.'

questions.q: Why does Julian tell the story of his reply about cathedrals?
options: To explain why he dislikes visiting cathedrals
To argue that the purist's ideal of quiet is recent
To show that cathedrals are no longer used
To insult the gentleman who had written to him
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Cuestiona el ideal purista: 'the quiet we revere is a rather recent invention'.

questions.q: What does Julian suggest by saying 'My producer would rather put a star on a poster'?
options: He believes the poster has no value
He dislikes his producer's choice of poster
He plans to put a star on the poster
He wryly notes that producers favour famous names
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Con humor, señala que al productor le interesa más un actor famoso que una buena frase.

questions.q: Julian says that verse makes modern settings impossible to accept.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'I think it's a surprisingly small problem.'

dictation: A modern setting is a gimmick when it's a costume the play doesn't fit.
Ask what the new setting lets the audience see, and if the answer is 'it's different', save your money.

title: Does Mass Tourism Erode Culture?

lines.text: Good evening. The motion: mass tourism does more to erode local culture than to sustain it. Professor Costa speaks in favour. Doctor Rao opposes. Professor, over to you.

Thank you. I'd like to start with a confession, which is that I'm a tourist. I've just come from a city where I queued forty minutes for a photograph of a fountain, and I can report that the fountain is fine. The city I'm less sure about.

What happens, I'd argue, is a slow shift in who a place is for. Shops that served neighbours become shops that serve visitors. Rents rise, residents leave, and what remains is a performance of the place rather than the place.

It's a moving picture, and not an inaccurate one for some districts. But I'd ask whether the alternative was ever a pristine, unchanging community. Places have always changed. Sometimes it's tourists that change them, and sometimes it's the road, the factory or the school.
Fair, but the pace matters. A culture can absorb change at one speed and be broken by another.

Agreed, which is why I'd talk about the management of tourism, not its existence. Where visitor numbers are limited and the revenue stays local, I've seen crafts revive that would otherwise have vanished.
I'd call that a museum economy. A craft that survives because it's decorative is surviving as an ornament.

That's a rather high standard for authenticity, Professor. Almost no living tradition meets it. A festival that was once for the village and now draws crowds is still a festival. Some of the people performing in it are still the village.
And others are paid to appear to be.
Some, certainly. Though I'd rather have a paid dancer than no dancer.
Professor Costa, that's a strong point. How do you respond?
I'd say it's the argument of every industry that has ever wanted to be thanked for what it has damaged. I'm not sure we should be so grateful.
I'd say it's the argument of someone who has already bought the plane ticket.
Touché. I did mention that I'm a tourist.
Is there any common ground?
Possibly in the idea that local people should decide. Not visitors, and not distant ministries.
I could sign that, with a footnote about whose voices count as local. A hotel owner and a retired teacher on the same street will not tell you the same thing.
No, and quite right too.
We'll leave it there. The vote will be taken after the break.

questions.q: What is Professor Costa's attitude to his own part in the problem he describes?
options: Angry at the city's long queues
Candid about being a tourist himself
Indifferent to the fountain's condition
Proud of the pleasure he has given
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Se incluye con franqueza en el fenómeno: 'I'd like to start with a confession, which is that I'm a tourist.'

questions.q: What does Doctor Rao imply by saying 'I'd rather have a paid dancer than no dancer'?
options: Tourists prefer paid performers
Authentic festivals no longer exist
An imperfect survival is better than none
Dancers should always be paid
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Prefiere una tradición imperfecta a su desaparición total.

questions.q: Professor Costa and Doctor Rao both accept that local people should have a say in decisions about tourism.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Rao propone que decidan los locales y Costa responde: 'I could sign that'.

questions.q: Why does Doctor Rao mention 'the road, the factory or the school'?
options: To show that tourism is not the only source of change
To argue that roads harm culture most
To list services that tourists need
To suggest that schools cause decline
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Relativiza el papel del turismo: 'Places have always changed.'

questions.q: What does Doctor Rao suggest by calling his argument 'the argument of someone who has already bought the plane ticket'?
options: She teases him for criticising what he himself does
She praises his willingness to travel
She suggests he is about to leave the debate
She accuses him of dishonest booking
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Le reprocha con humor la incoherencia, y él lo acepta: 'Touché. I did mention that I'm a tourist.'

questions.q: Doctor Rao says that places never changed before tourism.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'Places have always changed.'

dictation: A craft that survives because it's decorative is surviving as an ornament.
A culture can absorb change at one speed and be broken by another.

title: My House Is Cleverer Than Me

lines.text: Good evening. I'd like to tell you about my house, which, I should explain, is now cleverer than I am. It was sold to me as a smart home. I assumed this was a description of the house and not a warning.

The first thing I noticed was the lights. They come on when I enter a room, which is lovely, and turn off when I sit still for too long, which is less lovely, since reading is, as far as I know, a largely motionless activity.
I have therefore taken to waving at the ceiling every few minutes, like a man hailing a very slow taxi.

The thermostat has views of its own. It studies my habits and adjusts the temperature accordingly. It has, I think, concluded that I'm a man who enjoys being slightly cold, and I haven't the heart to tell it otherwise.

My refrigerator, meanwhile, has started sending me notifications. Last Tuesday it informed me that the door had been left open. I was standing in front of it at the time, so I felt it was a little unnecessary.
Then there's the voice assistant. I ask it for the weather and it tells me, in tones of enormous confidence, what the weather is in a town of the same name on the other side of the world.
I've begun to suspect that it enjoys this.

The manual, I should add, is a masterpiece of reassurance. It says, and I quote, that the system 'learns your preferences over time'. What it doesn't say is that your preferences, in the meantime, are being educated by a machine that has never been outdoors.
Now, I'm not complaining. I'm merely reporting. A good reporter keeps his feelings out of the story, which is why, if you've been following this talk, you'll have noticed that I'm furious.
The truth is that the technology works perfectly well when I do exactly what it expects. The difficulty arises whenever I behave like a human being, which, it turns out, is a deviation from the norm.

My neighbour, who is wiser than me, has a house with no smart devices at all. He has a switch, a thermostat with a dial and a window that he opens. He sleeps beautifully, and I confess to looking at his house with something close to envy.
I asked him once what he did when the lights failed. He said he turned on a lamp. I've thought about that conversation more than I'd like to admit.
Don't misunderstand me. I'm not proposing a return to candles. I like electricity and I like my house, in its way. I'd just like it to be a house and not a colleague.
Last week the assistant asked, unprompted, whether I needed anything. I said no. It said it was always here if I did. I've never felt so thoroughly supervised in my own kitchen.
So here is my advice. If you're offered a smart home, accept it only on the condition that it will switch off, politely and permanently, whenever you ask it to.
Thank you. If you'll excuse me, I have to wave at the ceiling, or the lights will go out on my applause.

questions.q: What is the speaker's attitude to the thermostat's mistaken conclusion about him?
options: Pride in its accurate learning
Anger at its dangerous errors
Determination to reprogram it tonight
Amused resignation towards its mistakes
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Lo acepta con resignación divertida: 'I haven't the heart to tell it otherwise.'

questions.q: What does he imply about the refrigerator's warning that the door was open?
options: The warning told him something he already knew
The alert came too late to be useful
He dislikes standing in the kitchen
The fridge door had actually been faulty
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Estaba delante de la puerta, así que el aviso sobraba: 'I was standing in front of it at the time'.

questions.q: The speaker's neighbour has a house without smart devices.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'has a house with no smart devices at all'.

questions.q: Why does he describe his neighbour's house?
options: To boast about his neighbour's wealth
To complain about his neighbour's noise
To advertise a particular thermostat
To suggest that simpler tools can serve better
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Contrasta la sencillez que funciona con su casa inteligente: 'He sleeps beautifully, and I confess to looking at his house with something close to envy.'

questions.q: What is the effect of saying that a good reporter keeps his feelings out of the story, 'which is why ... I'm furious'?
options: He deliberately contradicts his claim of detachment
He regrets expressing his feelings
He admires reporters' neutrality
He honestly hides his anger
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Dice no quejarse y a la vez deja claro que está furioso: 'I'm not complaining. I'm merely reporting.'

questions.q: The speaker wants to go back to using candles.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'I'm not proposing a return to candles.'

dictation: I have therefore taken to waving at the ceiling every few minutes, like a man hailing a very slow taxi.
I'd just like it to be a house and not a colleague.

title: Who Pays for the Play?

lines.text: Welcome to Cultural Matters. Tonight, a question that makes artists wince: should the arts be funded by the crowd? Callum Reid is a playwright who has just raised money online for his next production. Mei Chen advises a public arts fund. Callum, how did it go?

Better than I deserved, and worse than I'd hoped. We reached our target with two days to spare. But I spent five weeks sending messages that began, 'I know you're busy,' to people I'd rather have been having dinner with.
Which I'd call a fairly typical experience. Crowdfunding shifts the labour of fundraising to the artist, who is usually the least equipped for it.
And the most embarrassed. There's something peculiar about asking friends to pay for the privilege of watching you be creative.
Mei, is it democratic? The public chooses what it supports.

It's democratic in one sense, and conservative in another. The projects that do well tend to be the ones that are easy to explain in a sentence, with an appealing face and a ready-made audience. A difficult, strange piece of work finds it harder.
I'd confirm that. My successful campaign was for the most conventional play I'd written. I mention this with some shame.
Honesty becomes you.
So I'm told. It's never helped me with the bank.
Is there a case that the public fund has the same problem? Panels choosing what's worthy?

There is, and I'd rather admit it than pretend otherwise. Panels have their biases, and they're slower and less accountable than a crowd. What they can do is take a risk on work that nobody has asked for.
And that, for an artist, is the whole point. Nobody asked for the best plays. They were surprising, and surprise can't be pre-sold.
Quite. Which is why I'd see crowdfunding as a supplement. A way of finding out that people want a thing, once it exists.
Callum, would you do it again?

Yes, I think so, with a deep sigh, and a plan to spend a fraction of the time. I learned that the money isn't the only product. By the end I had two hundred people who'd paid to see the play, and I'd also acquired an audience. That's rarer than money.
That, I'd say, is the strongest argument for it.
A rare moment of agreement. Thank you both.

questions.q: What is Callum's attitude to his own crowdfunding campaign?
options: Relieved by the outcome but awkward about asking
Proud of how effortless it had been
Certain that he will never repeat it
Resentful of the friends who donated
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Se alegra del resultado pero le incomoda pedir dinero: 'Better than I deserved, and worse than I'd hoped.'

questions.q: What does Callum imply by saying that honesty 'has never helped me with the bank'?
options: Candour has not improved his finances
The bank refused his campaign money
He distrusts compliments from funders
He has never been honest with the bank
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Insinúa que la sinceridad no le da dinero: 'It's never helped me with the bank.'

questions.q: Callum's most successful campaign was for his most conventional play.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Lo dice así: 'My successful campaign was for the most conventional play I'd written.'

questions.q: Why does Mei say that panels can 'take a risk on work that nobody has asked for'?
options: To argue that artists should avoid panels
To show that panels never make mistakes
To explain what public funding can do that crowds cannot
To prove that crowds avoid all risk
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Defiende el papel propio de la financiación pública frente al crowdfunding.

questions.q: What does Callum suggest by 'the privilege of watching you be creative'?
options: He regrets having invited friends
He thinks creativity is a rare privilege
He mocks the idea that friends are honoured
He believes his friends are delighted to pay
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Habla de 'privilegio' con sarcasmo: pedir a los amigos que paguen por verle ser creativo resulta incómodo.

questions.q: Mei Chen says that panels are quicker and more accountable than crowds.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'they're slower and less accountable than a crowd'.

dictation: Crowdfunding shifts the labour of fundraising to the artist, who is usually the least equipped for it.
Nobody asked for the best plays.

title: The Quiet Contract of the Queue
focus: Wry humour, hedging and cultural observation

lines.text: Good morning. Today's topic is the queue, which I hope you'll agree is among the most underrated social institutions. I'd go so far as to say that a nation can be judged by the way it stands in a line, though I'm not sure which nation comes off best.

The mathematics first, because it's brief. In the simplest mathematical model, a single line feeding several counters is, on average, no faster than several separate lines. But it is fairer. The variation in waiting times falls, because nobody is stuck behind the customer with the mislaid receipt.

Notice what I said. On average, no faster. And yet people strongly prefer the single line. This tells you that what bothers us about waiting isn't only the length of it. It's the fear of being unlucky.

The psychologist David Maister wrote a well-known article on this in the nineteen eighties. His observations are now almost a creed in customer service. Occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time. Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones. Unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones.

Hence the mirrors by lifts, which is not a pleasant sentence, since it implies that we are being quietly managed. Mirrors give you something to do. Nobody has ever complained about waiting for a lift while adjusting a tie.
Hence also the screens at stations that tell you how long you have to wait. They do not make the train come sooner. They make the delay feel less like an insult.

Which is the key idea. A queue is a small contract. You give up your time, and in return you expect fairness. When somebody pushes in, it isn't the lost seconds that infuriate us. It's the breach of the contract.
I find it remarkable that most queues are policed without any official at all. People simply tut. Sometimes they sigh. In extreme cases, they say 'excuse me' in a tone that could strip paint.

There's a cultural dimension, naturally. In some places queues are rigid and in others they're closer to a gentle scrum. Neither is inferior. What matters is that everyone understands the rules, and the stranger who doesn't will be corrected within seconds.

I'd add a slightly worrying observation. Our tolerance for waiting has fallen. A delay that would have seemed trivial a generation ago now seems an affront. I don't think we've become less patient by nature. I think we've been trained to expect that waiting is an error rather than a feature of life.
Is that wholly bad? I'm not sure. Impatience has its virtues: it drives improvement. But it also makes us short-tempered with the person at the till, who's usually doing their best.
So let me suggest a modest experiment. The next time you find yourself in a long queue, don't reach for your phone. Look around. Notice how the line behaves.
You will, I think, see strangers cooperate without speaking, leave gaps for the unsteady and forgive an apology from the person in front. It is, in its quiet way, a small miracle.
And if all that fails to interest you, you'll at least have had a few minutes of uninterrupted thought, which is far rarer than it should be.
I'll stop here. I realise I've kept you for longer than most queues allow, and I'm grateful that nobody has said excuse me.
Thank you.

questions.q: What is the lecturer's attitude to modern impatience with waiting?
options: Wholly approving of rising impatience
Ambivalent, seeing both a benefit and a cost
Contemptuous of people who dislike waiting
Convinced that waiting was always unbearable
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Ve virtudes y costes: 'Impatience has its virtues' pero 'it also makes us short-tempered'.

questions.q: What does he imply by saying that mirrors by lifts are 'not a pleasant sentence'?
options: Lifts are slower in tall buildings
Designers quietly manipulate how waiting feels
Mirrors make lifts run faster
People dislike their own reflection
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Admite que se nos 'gestiona' sin saberlo: 'it implies that we are being quietly managed'.

questions.q: He says that a single line is fairer than several separate lines.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'But it is fairer. The variation in waiting times falls'.

questions.q: Why does he stress the words 'on average, no faster'?
options: To show that the preference is about fairness, not speed
To prove that single lines are slower
To criticise the mathematics of queueing
To suggest that shops cheat customers
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Muestra que no preferimos la cola única por rapidez: 'It's the fear of being unlucky.'

questions.q: How should the phrase 'in a tone that could strip paint' be understood?
options: As humorous exaggeration of a polite reproof
As a complaint about rude shop workers
As a recommendation for how to protest
As a literal warning about chemicals
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Es una hipérbole humorística sobre un 'excuse me' muy cortante.

questions.q: According to Maister's observations, unexplained waits feel shorter than explained ones.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'Unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones.'

dictation: A queue is a small contract.
They do not make the train come sooner.

title: Trained Memory Looks Like a Hunch

lines.text: My guest began playing chess at five and now teaches it for a living. Dmitri Volkov coaches junior players, several of whom would, I'm told, beat me in under a dozen moves. Dmitri, is that humbling or just accurate?
Both. And if it's any consolation, the quickest way to lose is to be certain you're winning.
Let's start with intuition. Strong players say they simply see the right move. Is that mystical?

Not at all, though I understand why it sounds so. Years of study leave a player with a vast library of patterns. When a position appears, a few candidate moves surface almost at once, and the player has the sensation of knowing without reasoning.
So intuition is really memory.

Memory that has been trained to look like a hunch. I'd add that it's reliable only in the area where it was trained. Ask a grandmaster to judge a business plan and the feeling of certainty is worth about as much as yours or mine.
Does it ever fail within chess?
Frequently. The classic error is to play the move that looks familiar rather than the one the position demands. A strong player is sometimes undone by their own pattern recognition.
How do you teach children to avoid that?
By asking them a boring question at every move: what has changed? What has my opponent just done? It sounds trivial, but nearly all blunders come from failing to check.
I'm told you also teach them to lose.

It's perhaps the most useful thing I do. A child who loses and analyses the game is learning far faster than one who wins easily and learns nothing. I tell the parents that I'm not coaching champions, I'm coaching people who can sit with a mistake.
Parents must love hearing that.
They nod politely and then ask when their child will be a grandmaster.
What about computers? Everyone knows they beat humans now.
They have done since the nineteen nineties, when a machine called Deep Blue defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov. Since then the machines have simply pulled further ahead.
Hasn't that made the game pointless?

On the contrary. Athletes run knowing that cars are faster. People play chess for the same reason they run: to find out what they can do. And the machines have given us wonderful tools for studying our mistakes.
Dmitri Volkov, thank you.
Thank you. And if you ever fancy a game, I promise to lose slowly.

questions.q: How does Dmitri explain the 'intuition' of strong players?
options: As trained pattern memory
As a mystical gift
As something that cannot be taught
As pure luck
questions.explain_es: Actitud. La desmitifica: 'Memory that has been trained to look like a hunch.'

questions.q: What does Dmitri imply by saying that a grandmaster's certainty about a business plan is 'worth about as much as yours or mine'?
options: Grandmasters are poor businesspeople by nature
Expertise in one field does not carry over to others
Hunches are useless in all fields
Business plans are simple to judge
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La intuición experta solo vale donde se entrenó: 'it's reliable only in the area where it was trained'.

questions.q: Dmitri says that intuition is reliable mainly in the field where it was trained.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'it's reliable only in the area where it was trained'.

questions.q: Why does Dmitri ask children 'what has changed?' at every move?
options: To discourage them from playing quickly
To keep them calm when they are losing
To make them check the position before moving
To test whether they remember the opening
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Busca que verifiquen antes de mover: 'nearly all blunders come from failing to check'.

questions.q: What does Dmitri imply when he says parents 'nod politely and then ask when their child will be a grandmaster'?
options: Parents refuse to listen to coaches
Parents agree that losing is valuable
Parents hear his point but still want results
Parents are angry about losing
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Los padres asienten por cortesía, pero siguen queriendo un campeón.

questions.q: Dmitri says that computers have made chess pointless.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Responde: 'On the contrary.'

dictation: Memory that has been trained to look like a hunch.
People play chess for the same reason they run: to find out what they can do.

title: Have We Lost Faith in Experts?

lines.text: Good evening. Tonight's motion: the public has lost faith in experts, and quite rightly so. Mister Kovac, a commentator, supports it. Professor Calloway, who studies the history of science, opposes. Mister Kovac, you have the floor.
Thank you, Chair. I'll start by saying that I rely on experts daily. I have a doctor, an accountant and a plumber, and I'd be unwise to argue with any of them about their business.

My objection is to the expert who strays beyond the evidence, who treats a forecast as a fact and a preference as a finding. Such people have been wrong in public, often at great cost, and have seldom been asked to explain.

I accept every word of that, which will surprise you. Experts have been wrong. Economists failed to foresee a major crisis; officials have underrated risks and overstated certainties. A profession that denied this would deserve to be mistrusted.
Then we agree, and I propose we all go home.
I'm afraid we don't, because the motion says the loss of faith is 'quite rightly so'. Distrusting an expert who's been wrong is rational. Distrusting all experts because some have been wrong is not.
That's a caricature of my position. I'm not recommending that people consult their cousins instead of surgeons.
I'm glad to hear it. Though I notice that in practice the loss of faith seldom stops at the economists. It spreads, and it's the vaccine specialist who ends up paying for the sins of the forecaster.
That's a serious charge, and I'd like to answer it. People can tell the difference between a field with a clear track record and one without. I'd have more faith in the public than you do.
It's a generous view and I'd like to share it. But the evidence suggests that people judge by tone more than by track record, and an expert who sounds arrogant is distrusted whatever their accuracy.
Then the remedy is humility, not blind deference.
On humility we're in total agreement. Experts who say 'we think' and 'we don't yet know' are, I'd argue, more trustworthy, though often less popular.
Mister Kovac, is that a concession?
It's a refinement. I'd say that the motion survives, with a small amendment: faith should be earned, and it's not wrong to withhold it until then.
A good deal of the motion has quietly left the building.
A good deal of mine has too, I admit. But the amendment is the part that matters.
On that cheerful note of mutual erosion, we'll go to the audience.

questions.q: What is Mister Kovac's stance towards experts at the start of the debate?
options: He considers experts always accurate
He distrusts every expert on principle
He prefers amateur advice to professional advice
He respects experts but objects to overreaching
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Confía en los expertos en su campo pero critica a quien se sale de la evidencia: 'I rely on experts daily' y 'strays beyond the evidence'.

questions.q: What does Professor Calloway imply by saying that 'the vaccine specialist ... ends up paying for the sins of the forecaster'?
options: The public trusts only specialists in health
Vaccine specialists are the least reliable
Mistrust spreads to experts who did nothing wrong
Forecasters never apologise for errors
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La desconfianza hacia un grupo se extiende a otros inocentes: 'it spreads'.

questions.q: Professor Calloway says that experts who admit uncertainty may be more trustworthy.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'Experts who say 'we think' and 'we don't yet know' are, I'd argue, more trustworthy'.

questions.q: Why does Mister Kovac say 'I'm not recommending that people consult their cousins instead of surgeons'?
options: To confess that he distrusts surgeons
To show he has a large family
To reject the caricature of his position
To argue that family advice is reliable
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Rechaza que su postura se reduzca a una caricatura: 'That's a caricature of my position.'

questions.q: What does the chair imply by 'a cheerful note of mutual erosion'?
options: That Professor Calloway won the debate
That both speakers have given up part of their positions
That the motion was formally withdrawn
That the audience has left the hall
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Resume con humor que ambos han cedido terreno: 'A good deal of the motion has quietly left the building.'

questions.q: Mister Kovac says that people should consult their relatives instead of surgeons.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'I'm not recommending that people consult their cousins instead of surgeons.'

dictation: Distrusting an expert who's been wrong is rational.
Distrusting all experts because some have been wrong is not.
